strengths: Originality: The cotangent lift of a constrained autoencoder provides a useful construction for nonlinear dimensionality reduction with exact symplectic embeddings and encoder–decoder consistency. Propositions 1–2 explain how these properties follow from the configuration-space projection identities.

Significance: Jointly learning a reduced representation and Hamiltonian dynamics addresses a relevant limitation of conventional HNNs. The experiments include conservative, nonseparable, and dissipative systems, reaching 600 configuration dimensions.

Empirical merits: Table 2 shows improved pendulum reconstruction and prediction relative to the tested reduction methods. Appendix H.3 adds cloth reduction and joint-training ablations, while Table 5 reports a roughly 3.8-fold inference speedup over the 15-DoF HNN.

Presentation and reproducibility: The overall architecture is understandable, and the appendices provide substantial information about simulation parameters, network sizes, initialization, learning rates, and training horizons. The simulated physical-system experiments raise no apparent material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—conservation claims exceed the guarantees. Section 3 states that learning a valid reduced Hamiltonian preserves the original reduced energy E composed with the embedding. However, the learned Hamiltonian is not constrained to equal that pullback. Its continuous flow conserves its own learned energy; symplecticity alone does not establish conservation of the physical energy or inheritance of the original system’s stability. These distinctions are central to the paper’s claims and require correction or additional assumptions and evidence.

Soundness and reproducibility—the integration procedure is insufficiently specified. Appendix E derives only conservative Hamiltonian subflows, although the method also integrates damping and external contact forces. General dissipative flows are not symplectic, and the manuscript does not provide the actual update rules or justify their properties. Moreover, Eq. (35) uses a half-step for the central binding flow rather than the full step in standard Strang splitting; Eqs. (30) and (32) contain incorrect signs or derivatives. These could be transcription errors, but the implemented algorithm cannot be established reliably from the description.

Evaluation—the strongest cloth extrapolation evidence is ambiguous. Figures 12–13 explicitly state that ground truth beyond 0.3 seconds is extrapolated from the last observation, whereas Appendix G.3 describes test simulations extending to 0.5 seconds. Extrapolated targets do not validate physical prediction accuracy. The source of contact forces during test rollouts is also unclear: supplying recorded forces would establish conditional prediction rather than autonomous contact simulation.

Comparative evidence does not adequately isolate the proposed advantages. The pendulum transformation is generated using the same constrained-autoencoder family employed by the method (Appendix G.1.1). The weakly symplectic baseline uses independent position and momentum autoencoders, restricting their coupling. The Cholesky comparison changes network sharing and widths as well as matrix parametrization. There is also no direct comparison with the closely related reduced-order Lagrangian approach of Friedl et al. (2025). These choices weaken claims that the gains specifically establish the importance of the proposed geometry.

Significance and limitations—the results support a narrower claim than accurate, generalizable high-dimensional dynamics at scale. Table 3 reports approximately 40–46% relative vortex errors, and Table 1 reports approximately 71% long-horizon pendulum position error. Timing is provided only for the 15-DoF example, without training cost or scaling measurements on the larger systems. All examples assume strong reducibility; the discussion should address this restriction, contact-force availability, and the distinction between longer rollouts and generalization to new physical regimes.

Reproducibility and presentation contain material inconsistencies. Appendix G.2 specifies vortex latent dimensions 3 and 6 and an input layer of size 600, while the main experiment uses dimensions 6 and 10 for a 90-DoF system. No implementation link, hardware specification, or variability across training seeds is supplied. Reported standard deviations describe test trajectories rather than optimization robustness. The appendix detail is valuable, but these discrepancies must be resolved before the results can be reproduced confidently.

Originality is concentrated in the symplectic autoencoder and its integration into the learning pipeline: the constrained autoencoder, Riemannian optimization, SPD network, and extended-phase-space integrator substantially build on cited methods. This can constitute a useful contribution, but the unresolved theoretical and evaluation issues currently prevent a convincing demonstration of its added value.

strengths: Originality: The cotangent lift of a constrained autoencoder is a useful extension of existing reduced-order learning methods. Propositions 1–2 provide a concrete construction satisfying the decoder’s symplecticity and the encoder–decoder projection identities, rather than merely penalizing their violation.

Significance: Learning nonlinear reduced Hamiltonian dynamics is a worthwhile problem. The experiments cover conservative, nonseparable, and dissipative systems, including a 600-DoF cloth. Table 5 reports a useful inference-time reduction from 100.25 ms for the full pendulum HNN to 26.34 ms for RO-HNN.

Evaluation: The paper includes several informative ablations of reduction methods, Hamiltonian parametrizations, integrators, and joint training. Table 2 supports improved reconstruction and short-horizon prediction on the constructed pendulum benchmark, while the cloth experiments demonstrate promising position accuracy.

Presentation and reproducibility: The overall architecture is understandable, and the appendices provide substantial information about simulation settings, initialization, network sizes, and optimization. The restriction to canonical systems with low-dimensional approximations is stated explicitly. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—overstated preservation guarantees: Section 3 treats a valid learned latent Hamiltonian as sufficient to preserve the original reduced energy E composed with the embedding. It guarantees conservation of the learned Hamiltonian in continuous conservative dynamics, but does not establish its equality to the physical Hamiltonian’s pullback. Likewise, a symplectic embedding alone does not guarantee the original system’s other conservation laws or stability properties. These distinctions undermine central claims in the introduction and conclusion; the paper needs narrower guarantees and direct validation of physical invariants.

Soundness and reproducibility—integrator specification: Appendix E contains substantive inconsistencies: Eqs. (30) and (32) have incorrect signs or differentiation variables, and Eq. (35) uses a half-step for the central coupling flow rather than the full step in the stated Strang composition. The text also says w ≤ 0 while its SoftPlus parametrization is positive. More importantly, the appendix describes conservative Hamiltonian flows without specifying how damping and external forces in Eq. (11) enter the algorithm. Those forces generally destroy symplecticity. The actual implemented solver and the scope of its guarantees therefore remain unclear.

Evaluation—long-horizon evidence is ambiguous: Captions for Figures 12–13 explicitly state that ground truth beyond the training interval is extrapolated from the last observation, whereas Appendix G.3 describes test simulations extending to 0.5 seconds. These accounts need reconciliation before the cloth extrapolation claims can be assessed. For the vortex, Section 4.2 reports a prediction horizon H = 100 while Appendix G.2 gives a 0.001-second timestep, yet figures span 15 seconds. Whether predictions restart from observed states or run continuously is not explained. The cloth reduction comparison in Figure 14 uses only a 0.0025-second horizon.

Evaluation—comparisons do not isolate the claimed advantages: The pendulum’s nonlinear coordinate transformation is generated using the same constrained-autoencoder family employed by the proposed method (Appendix G.1.1), favoring its inductive bias. The weakly symplectic baseline uses independent position and momentum autoencoders, whereas the proposed momentum decoder depends on position, confounding expressivity with hard versus soft constraint enforcement. The Cholesky comparison also changes network width and parameter sharing. Stronger matched comparisons, including the closely related reduced-order Lagrangian approach on mechanical tasks, are needed.

Significance and limitations: The results support a narrower claim than accurate, generalizable high-dimensional dynamics learning. Table 1 reports approximately 0.71 mean relative position error for the five-second pendulum rollout, and Table 3 reports approximately 0.40–0.46 errors for the geometric vortex models. The cloth model requires measured constraint forces, but their availability and evaluation during prediction are insufficiently explained. Scaling evidence is limited to a runtime comparison on the 15-DoF pendulum; training cost, memory, hardware, and scaling on the larger systems are not reported.

Reproducibility and presentation: Appendix G.2 specifies vortex latent dimensions 3 and 6 and an input layer of size 600, conflicting with the 90-DoF system and dimensions 6 and 10 reported in the main experiments. Eq. (6) has the wrong sign for the momentum target, and Section 3.2 uses the encoder where the decoder is required. These errors, together with the solver ambiguities, prevent confident reimplementation. Reported standard deviations describe test trajectories, without establishing robustness across training seeds.

Originality and interpretation: Much of the pipeline explicitly reuses prior constrained autoencoders, SPD networks, Riemannian training, and extended-phase-space integration. The cotangent-lift construction is the clearest contribution, but the broader claim that Cholesky parametrization causes inaccurate dynamics through flawed distance measures is not established by the trajectory-loss formulation or the confounded ablation. Overall, the useful construction does not outweigh the unresolved guarantee and evaluation issues.

strengths: Originality: The cotangent-lifted autoencoder is a useful architectural contribution. Combining a configuration-space encoder–decoder pair satisfying exact projection identities with the momentum lift produces a symplectic embedding by construction. Propositions 1–2 substantiate this structural guarantee.

Significance: Jointly learning a nonlinear reduced representation and Hamiltonian dynamics addresses a meaningful limitation of conventional HNNs. The experiments cover conservative mechanics, vortex dynamics, and forced dissipative cloth dynamics, including a 600-DoF system.

Empirical support: Table 2 shows improved reconstruction and short-horizon prediction over linear, quadratic, and weakly symplectic reductions. Appendix H.3 provides additional cloth comparisons and joint-training ablations. Table 5 reports approximately 3.8-fold faster evaluation than the full-order pendulum HNN.

Presentation and reproducibility: The overall architecture is understandable, Figure 1 is helpful, and the appendices provide substantial information about data generation, network architectures, initialization, and optimization. The manuscript appropriately credits the existing constrained autoencoder, SPD network, and integration methods on which it builds.
weaknesses: Soundness—conservation claims exceed the guarantees: Section 3 asserts that learning a valid reduced Hamiltonian preserves the physical reduced energy E composed with the embedding. A learned Hamiltonian conserves its own value under exact conservative dynamics; symplecticity alone does not establish equality with the pullback of the true Hamiltonian, preservation of the original system's other invariants, or stability. The non-intrusive training objective does not enforce that equality. The paper needs to distinguish its valid architectural guarantee from these stronger physical claims.

Soundness and reproducibility—the numerical method is insufficiently specified: Appendix E describes only conservative Hamiltonian subflows, although the cloth experiments integrate damping and external contact forces. The force updates and their numerical properties are not given, and a dissipative flow is generally not symplectic. The appendix also contains substantive formula inconsistencies: incorrect signs/derivatives in Equations 30 and 32, a half-step rather than full-step central flow in Equation 35 relative to the stated Strang splitting, and a claim that a positive SoftPlus parametrization enforces w <= 0. These require correction and verification against the implementation.

Evaluation—the long-horizon cloth evidence is ambiguous: Appendix G.3 says test trajectories are simulated to 0.5 seconds, but Figures 12–13 explicitly state that ground truth beyond 0.3 seconds is extrapolated from the last observation. This discrepancy directly affects the claimed extrapolation accuracy and energy agreement. The paper must establish which results use independently simulated ground truth. It must also explain whether test-time contact forces are supplied from reference trajectories or recomputed from predicted states, since these imply different prediction tasks.

Significance and external validity—the strongest conclusions are broader than the evaluation: The pendulum benchmark is deliberately made reducible and transformed using the same constrained-autoencoder family employed by the method. This is useful as a controlled experiment but favors its inductive bias. Runtime evidence is restricted to 15 DoF, without training cost, memory, hardware, or scaling measurements for the larger systems. Vortex relative errors remain around 0.40–0.46, and Table 1 reports a long-horizon pendulum position error around 0.71, warranting more qualified claims of accurate generalization.

Attribution of gains to geometry is not adequately isolated: Appendix G.1 uses separate 32-wide networks for the proposed geometric HNN but a shared 64-wide architecture for the Cholesky baseline. Consequently, the comparison changes more than the SPD parametrization. Table 4 also does not show uniform superiority of the SPD damping network. Matched architectures, repeated training seeds, and uncertainty across runs are needed to support the claim that geometric treatment itself explains the gains.

Reproducibility and limitations: The vortex training description specifies latent dimensions {3, 6} and a 600-dimensional input layer, conflicting with the 90-DoF experiment using {6, 10}. No accompanying implementation or training-seed variability is identified. The discussion should more clearly delimit the assumed low-dimensional reducibility, restricted cotangent-lift representation, and dependence on observed forces. I see no material research-ethics concern in the simulated experiments; the decisive concerns are technical and evidential.
